title: Gastronomia bisneksenä: Sami Koponen kertoo maisteriohjelmasta
content:
Sami Koponen is a member of the steering group for the new Master’s Programme in International Food Business and Gastronomy and works in the Department of Economics and Management at the Faculty of Agriculture and Forestry.

1. Sami, what does “gastronomy” mean in practice for this master’s programme, and what concrete skills do students gain?

– Gastronomy can be defined in many ways; it is a highly multidisciplinary concept. In this master’s programme we maintain that breadth while placing particular emphasis on the commercial application of gastronomic understanding. We look at gastronomy especially from the perspective of high value food markets. Students learn to analyse how added value is created in relation to current gastronomic themes such as sustainability, authenticity and distinctiveness.

2. How does a university level food business master’s programme differ from culinary and restaurant education?

title: Researchers map which gene versions brain cells use, cell by cell
content:
In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins. 

Not all changes in isoforms have a visible effect. Sometimes, however, the wrong version can have drastic consequences. Incorrect isoforms have been associated with several brain diseases, including ALS, frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. 

“In these diseases, a protein named TDP-43 leaves its normal place in the cell and forms clumps, so it can no longer do its job," describes , University Researcher at the Department of Computer Science, University of Helsinki. 

"As a result, certain RNAs are spliced incorrectly, and neuronal cells lose proteins they need.” 

Detecting faulty splicing in the brain is not easy. Researchers at the University of Helsinki and  have now developed a method that maps which gene isoforms the cells in brain tissue use. In the future, it can also be used to identify faulty splicing. 

For this work, the team engineered new laboratory techniques as well as algorithms, software and statistical tools for analysing the data.

title: Latest updates on the HiLIFE tenure track call
content:
The most recent HiLIFE tenure track call for assistant/associate professors has closed on November 16, 2026. We were thrilled to receive a record-breaking total of 745 applications. 

A significant number of applications were sent in from the following locations: Finland (192), the United States (103), Germany (70), and Sweden (47). The same countries were also topping our statistics in the previous Tenure Track calls. Based on the applicants’ responses, the most represented primary ERC LS panels were LS8, LS1, and LS5.

The Appointment Committee will soon begin the first-stage evaluation; the applicants can expect to receive the results by mid-March 2027.

Following the initial evaluation, the shortlisted candidates will go through a 2nd stage external evaluation during March - April 2027. Selected applicants are then invited to interviews held in late May – early June 2027. 

The entire recruitment process is due to be finalized in September 2027, with the announcement of new HiLIFE tenure track assistant and associate professors.

If you have any questions about the recruitment, please contact hilife-recruit(at)helsinki.fi.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Maapallon metsistä koottiin tähän asti tarkin 3D-kartasto
content:

The five-year project, led by the University of Bristol, brought together thousands of airborne LiDAR surveys of forested landscapes across the world. LiDAR is a laser scanning technology that can create detailed 3D maps of both vegetation and the underlying terrain across hundreds of square kilometres.

The atlas opens up new opportunities to map forest carbon stocks and to guide biodiversity conservation and restoration efforts. Researchers from more than 100 institutions worldwide took part in the project.

The University of Helsinki group contributed LiDAR data and the biomass and carbon models derived from it for the Taita Hills in Kenya. Professor of Geoinformatics and his colleagues in y have carried out remote sensing research in the area for two decades. “It is wonderful that our unique dataset, collected in the 2010s with funding from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland, keeps finding new uses,” Pellikka says.

The atlas is an important tool for research.

title: Journal of Hegemony, Emotions, Populism and Polarisation
content:
The Journal of Hegemony, Emotions, Populism, and Polarisation publishes studies on how meanings, actions, and habits are structured by affect, power dynamics, and collective identities. We invite diverse theoretical viewpoints on emotions, hegemony, polarisation, nationalism, and populism—across various modes and at scales from the intimate to the global. We welcome novel methodological contributions, which include computational social sciences, constructivist, pragmatist, and semiotic approaches, discourse theory, multimodal analysis, and post-foundational hegemony research. 

Understanding political meaning-making and knowledge structures is crucial for navigating contemporary society and its power relations. To grasp the hegemonic contestations, contributions to the journal could take into account the politics surrounding the platformization of society, the global impact of algorithmic environments, and the growing inequalities within the knowledge economy. For this reason, social media, g/local hybrid struggles, and community building are topics of special interest to the journal.

title: Lizards build complex teeth differently to humans
content:
Researchers from the Institute of Biotechnology, part of the Helsinki Institute of Life Science (HiLIFE) at the University of Helsinki, have shown how evolution can produce similarly complex tooth shapes through very different biological mechanisms.

Understanding how organs acquire their shape during development is a key research focus in biology and evolution.

Teeth are an excellent case study as their shapes are closely linked to what animals eat and how they have adapted to different environments over millions of years. 

Until now, it was debate swirled around the assumption that vertebrates using many of the same genes to produce complex tooth shapes also used the same mechanism. This new study led by Research Director Dr Nicolas Di-Poi has uncovered how evolution can use the same genetic toolkit in different ways, ending the debate.

“We discovered that nature has more than one way to build a complex tooth. Even though mammals and lizards use many of the same genes, they organise these signals differently during development,” Dr Di-Poi said.

title: Part 1: Daniele Soares' Rebuilding Jerusalem: Labor and Taxation in Ezra-Nehemiah
content:
Daniele Soares is a Brazilian scholar and doctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki. Her interdisciplinary journey from economics to theology, anthropology, and cultural studies reflects a longstanding interest in understanding the relationship between people, society, and faith. Her current research examines labor and taxation in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah during Jerusalem’s post-exilic rebuilding.

title: 7 Dec, 6pm: Open Talk on the Social Contract and US Politics: Kirsten Fischer and Charles Postel (CO3 and HEPP event)
content:
Helsinki Hub on Emotions Populism and Polarisation Keynote Seminar in 2026 by 

Charles Postel and Kirsten Fischer:

US Politics at the Crossroads: The Meaning of the “Blue Wave” Midterms and the Way Ahead

Since January of 2025, the second Trump administration has waged an assault on the American social contract. It has wielded federal power against universities, law firms, and the media. It has gutted public health, science, foreign aid, and the social safety net. It has sent the military into cities to intimidate its critics, and it has unleashed a cruel and reckless program of mass deportation against immigrant communities. It has upended global trade, conducted extrajudicial killings at sea, and launched an unprovoked war against Iran. And at every turn, policy has served the corrupt purpose of enriching the Trump family and aligned billionaires.
